opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting middle ground, and I think it's one of the reasons I've stayed at Ai2.

Compared with academia, the biggest difference is resources and focus. In a university lab you have a lot of intellectual freedom, but you're often constrained by compute, by the need for every student to have their own first-author paper, and by the publication cycle. That pushes people toward smaller, more incremental projects. At Ai2 we can do things that look more like what the frontier labs do: train full models end to end, build the pretraining data, the post-training recipes, the evaluation suites, and release all of it. You need a team of dozens of people working on one artifact for that, and academia isn't really set up to reward that kind of collective work.

Compared with the closed labs, the freedom is almost the opposite. At a place like OpenAI or Anthropic or Google, you have enormous compute and very talented people, but what you can say publicly is tightly controlled. A lot of the most interesting results never see the light of day because they're competitive advantages. For us, openness is the point. We release the weights, the data, the training code, the intermediate checkpoints. I can write about what worked and what didn't on my blog, and I can talk about it on podcasts like this. That's a kind of freedom you just don't get inside a closed lab.

The trade-off is that we're always resource-constrained relative to the frontier. We have to be very deliberate about which bets we make. We can't run a hundred big experiments and keep the best one. So the freedom is real, but it's freedom with a strong sense of mission: we're trying to show that the whole recipe for a strong model can be done in the open, and that the research community benefits when it can actually study these systems rather than just poke at them through an API.

To me, that mix of a real mission, reasonable resources, and the ability to share everything is pretty rare. I don't think it's strictly better than either alternative for everyone, but for someone who cares about the open ecosystem, it's the best seat in the house.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because Ai2 really sits in this weird middle ground. In academia, you have a ton of freedom on paper, like you can work on whatever you want, but you're constrained by compute and by the incentive structure. You need to publish, your students need to graduate, and realistically you can't train a frontier-ish language model on a few dozen GPUs. So the freedom is real but the scope is narrow.

At the closed labs, it's kind of the opposite. You have enormous resources, but the research agenda is increasingly set by the product. Even the stuff that does get published is filtered through what's commercially sensitive, so a lot of the most interesting findings just never leave the building. And I think a lot of researchers there feel that, especially people who came up through the open science culture of the 2010s.

Ai2's position is that we're a nonprofit with actual compute, and our mission is to release everything, the weights, the data, the code, the training recipes. So for me, working on OLMo and Tülu, the freedom isn't just "I can pick my topic," it's that the whole point of the work is to make it legible to other people. I don't have to ask whether something is okay to share. The default is yes.

That said, I don't want to oversell it. We have constraints too. We're a smaller organization, so we have to pick our battles. We're not going to out-scale OpenAI or Google, so a lot of the freedom comes with the responsibility to be strategic about where open research actually adds value. Post-training, data, evaluation, those are places where openness really moves the field, because nobody else is showing their work there.

So I'd say the freedom at Ai2 is less about doing anything you want and more about being able to do the work fully, end to end, in public. For the kind of researcher I am, that's the version of freedom that matters most.

astra-6.text:
I think Ai2 occupies a really interesting middle ground. We have a lot of the intellectual freedom that people associate with academia, but we also have a team of engineers and the resources to build things together. If you want to study language models, that infrastructure matters enormously. It’s hard to do everything with a professor and a few graduate students, especially when the professor is also teaching and writing grants.

At a closed lab, you might have much more compute, but your research ultimately has to fit the company’s priorities. And there’s a separate question of what you can share. You could have freedom to explore something internally without being able to publish the details that would let someone else build on it.

For me, the appeal of Ai2 is that openness is part of the mission. The paper, the model, and the explanation of how we built it can all be part of the contribution. That doesn’t mean unlimited resources or no constraints—we still have to choose what’s worth doing. But there’s a lot of room to pursue work because we think it will help the research community understand these systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Ai2 occupies a really interesting middle ground. In academia, you have a lot of intellectual freedom, but you’re often constrained by compute, funding, and the time you spend writing grants or teaching. At a closed AI lab, you have tremendous resources, but your research ultimately has to fit the company’s priorities, and you may not be able to share what you learn.

At Ai2, we can work on substantial models while making the research public—the models, the data, the training process, and the lessons along the way. That openness is a big part of the appeal for me. There are still constraints; we have to choose where to spend our compute and what projects are worth pursuing. But there’s a lot of room to follow a research question and produce something that people outside the organization can actually build on.
